title: Google Ships Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 With 4K Output and Half-Price API
subtitle: Google's updated image model went generally available on October 6, cutting per-image API costs about 50% and adding mask-based editing.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google promoted `gemini-nano-banana-2.1` to general availability on October 6, 2026, with Google Cloud documentation listing it as the stable image model. It accepts text, image, video, and PDF inputs and returns image and text outputs, up to 4K resolution with 1K as the default. The release adds mask-based editing — users can constrain changes to a selected region — along with better prompt adherence, improved text rendering, and multi-image fusion for up to 14 reference images (including up to four people and ten objects that need to look consistent). Google is positioning it as an efficient complement to Gemini 3 Pro Image rather than a replacement.

The pricing change is the sharpest signal. On the Gemini API, a 1K image now costs roughly 3.4 cents versus 6.7 cents previously, and a 4K image costs about 7.6 cents versus 15.1 cents. Batch jobs come down further. Combined with mask editing, which lets apps iterate on specific regions instead of regenerating a whole image, the per-task cost of image workflows at the top end drops meaningfully. Rollout covers the Gemini app, AI Mode in Google Search, Google Ads, and developer tools including AI Studio, Flow, and Stitch.

This continues a pattern the frontier labs have been running all autumn — small, cheaper image and multimodal updates arriving every few weeks instead of once a year. OpenAI's visual-ads test, Meta's Hatch agent, and now Nano Banana 2.1 all push the same direction: image generation becomes a utility, folded into other products, at utility prices. Anthropic's own Haiku 5.5 move earlier this week fits the same template on the text side. Pricing cuts of 50% to 75% are no longer rare one-time events; they are becoming the quarterly cadence.

A takeaway for learners: image generation is tipping from a standalone product into a feature inside other software. If you are learning to build with these models, spend time on mask-based editing and multi-image fusion rather than only on single-shot prompt-to-image. Those are the primitives real applications — storefronts, ad tools, design assistants — actually use. The prompt-only workflow still exists, but it is now the simplest case, not the frontier.
